title: Pappardelle ai funghi misti
subtitle: Wide ribbon pasta with mixed mushrooms and parsley
excerpt: Pappardelle ai funghi misti pairs the widest of the ribbon pastas with a quick, intensely flavoured mushroom sauce built on dried porcini and chestnut mushrooms. The dish comes together in about 30 minutes and works as a weeknight dinner or a relaxed first course. A handful of flat-leaf parsley and a scrape of Parmesan pull it together at the end.
sourceNotes: Italian home-cooking tradition. Mushroom ragù with pappardelle is a staple of Tuscany and the wider north-Italian kitchen. Techniques drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992), and Giuliano Bugialli, The Fine Art of Italian Cooking (1977).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The mushroom sauce keeps in the fridge for two days. Reheat gently with a splash of pasta water before tossing with freshly cooked pappardelle.

glossaryTerms.definition: The flavoured liquid left after soaking dried mushrooms or other dried ingredients in warm water; adds concentrated depth to sauces and braises.
Italian for 'to the tooth': pasta cooked until it still offers a little resistance when bitten, not soft all the way through.

content.text: Pappardelle ai funghi misti is a mushroom sauce built on two kinds of fungus: dried porcini for depth and chestnut mushrooms for body. The wide pasta ribbons hold the sauce in their folds and carry each mouthful cleanly to the fork. The whole thing is on the table in about 30 minutes.
Rehydrating the porcini is the key step. Keep the
soaking liquor
: it carries the porcini flavour and doubles as the braising liquid for the sauce. Pour it in slowly and leave the gritty sediment at the bottom of the bowl.
What you need

items.prepNote: soaked in 250 ml warm water for 20 minutes
finely grated, plus more to serve

content.text: You need a large frying pan wide enough to toss the pasta in at the end. A sauté pan or a wide shallow casserole works equally well.
Method
Soak the porcini

Put {{mushrooms-porcini-dried}} of dried porcini into a small bowl and cover with 250 ml of warm water. Leave for 20 minutes. Lift the porcini out with a slotted spoon, squeeze gently, and chop roughly. Set the soaking liquid aside; you will use most of it in the sauce.
Build the mushroom sauce

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil and {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the shallots and cook for 5 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Turn the heat to high. Add {{chestnut-mushrooms}} of sliced chestnut mushrooms and the chopped porcini. Cook without stirring for 3 minutes to get some colour, then toss and cook for 2 minutes more.

Pour in {{dry-white-wine}} of dry white wine. Let it bubble and reduce by half, about 2 minutes. Then add the porcini soaking liquid, pouring slowly and leaving the last tablespoon of gritty sediment behind. Simmer for 5 minutes until the sauce has a light coating consistency. Season with salt and black pepper.
Cook the pasta and finish
Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to the boil. Cook {{pasta-dried}} of pappardelle until
al dente
, usually 1 minute less than the packet says. Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining.

Tip the drained pasta into the mushroom pan. Toss over medium heat, adding a splash of pasta water to loosen if needed. Add most of the parsley and half the Parmesan, toss again, then serve immediately with more Parmesan and a grinding of black pepper.

items.cause: Too much porcini soaking liquid added, or pasta water over-loosened the sauce.
items.fix: Simmer the sauce on its own for 2 minutes before adding the pasta, or reduce with the pasta over higher heat for 1 minute.

items.cause: Left in the colander too long before adding to the sauce.
items.fix: Move the pasta to the sauce immediately after draining. If it has stuck, add 50 ml of pasta water and toss briskly over heat.

items.cause: Not enough seasoning, or the porcini soaking water was discarded.
items.fix: Add more salt a little at a time. A teaspoon of lemon juice lifts the whole dish if the mushroom flavour has gone muddy.

items.symptom: Mushrooms are watery rather than golden
items.cause: Pan was not hot enough or too crowded, so they steamed instead of browning.
items.fix: Cook in two batches next time, or increase the heat and resist stirring for the first 3 minutes.

content.text: Variations

A splash of double cream stirred in at the end makes the sauce richer. Fresh thyme or tarragon works in place of the parsley. Tagliatelle or fettuccine are natural alternatives to pappardelle. For a vegan version, leave out the butter and Parmesan and finish with a little more olive oil and a handful of toasted pine nuts.
Where this dish lives

Pappardelle with mushrooms is a Tuscan and Emilian staple. Wide ribbon pasta and autumn mushrooms have gone together in this kitchen for centuries. The dried-porcini trick works because the soaking water carries the same earthy depth as a mushroom stock, at no extra effort. Made in October when chestnut mushrooms are at their best, the dish tastes of the season.
